etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Medieval Latin incentīvus (“that strikes up or sets the tune”), from incinō (“to strike up”), from in- (“in, on”) + canō (“to sing”). The formation appears to have been influenced by incendō (“to set on fire”).

definitions.definition: Something that motivates, rouses, or encourages.

quote.citation: 2013 June 7, David Simpson, “Fantasy of navigation”, in The Guardian Weekly‎[1], volume 188, number 26, page 36:
quote.text: It is tempting to speculate about the incentives or compulsions that might explain why anyone would take to the skies in [the] basket [of a balloon]: perhaps out of a desire to escape the gravity of this world or to get a preview of the next; […].

definitions.definition: A bonus or reward, often monetary, to work harder.
Inciting; encouraging or moving; rousing to action; stimulating.

quote.citation: 1667, attributed to Richard Allestree, The Causes of the Decay of Christian Piety. […], London:  […]  R. Norton for T. Garthwait, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Competency is of all other proportions the most incentive to industry.

definitions.definition: Serving to kindle or set on fire.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VI”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Part incentive reed / Provide, pernicious with one touch of fire.
